name: Mallord Street
rooms: The front door opens into a narrow hall that runs the depth of the house to the wide timber staircase at the back. The stair is the original, with turned balusters and a heavy carved newel. Both reception rooms open off the hall, and a cloakroom sits beneath the landing.

At the front of the ground floor, with two tall windows onto the street and a fireplace on the party wall. The floor is the original oak, and the shelving either side of the chimney was made by the present owners. A dining room behind it looks down the garden.

The owners added the kitchen at garden level, across the whole back of the house. A long table stands in front of a pair of glazed timber doors that open straight onto the terrace. The room gets the sun from late morning, and a guest bedroom and shower room are at the front of this floor.

The garden faces south and runs eighteen metres from the kitchen doors. A stone terrace gives way to a long lawn between planted borders, with two old trees at the far end. It is one of the quietest gardens on the street.

The front of the first floor, with timber panelling on two walls and a pair of tall windows hung with heavy linen. The floorboards are the originals. The bathroom is across the landing, and the study is behind.

One of the two bathrooms the owners added, with a freestanding bath under a sash window and a long timber vanity built in the workshop. The floor is wide oak boards, treated for water. It serves the principal bedroom.

At the back of the first floor, where the writer of the household worked. A long desk runs under a row of windows that look down the garden, with bookshelves on the inner wall. It is the room with the best light in the afternoon.
At the back of the top floor, under the slope of the roof, with a window over the garden. Pale oak boards and plain white walls keep it simple. A third bedroom and a shower room share this floor.

The reason the house was built: a studio across the whole front of the top floor, lit by a tall north window that gives the even light painters wanted. The present owners used it as a furniture workshop. It is a room that could become almost anything, and is best left as it is.
